lane.name: Velvet Underground and proto-indie
lane.definition: The Velvet Underground, Lou Reed, Nico, the Modern Lovers/Jonathan Richman: drone, deadpan and amateurism as virtues.

albums.label: Verve Records
albums.description: Nico's debut strands her deep, accented alto in chamber-folk arrangements of songs written for her by Jackson Browne, Lou Reed, John Cale, and Tim Hardin, plus strings and flute overdubs added by producer Tom Wilson without her input, which she said she hated. 'These Days' and 'Chelsea Girls' pair her flat, funereal phrasing with delicate fingerpicked guitar, more accessible than the Velvet Underground but just as melancholy. It is the folkiest record she ever made before turning toward the harmonium-driven drone of her later albums.
albums.lineage: Written largely by her Velvet Underground and Greenwich Village circle, the album is the folk-pop bridge between the Velvets' orbit and Nico's own turn toward stark, avant-garde songwriting on The Marble Index.

albums.label: Verve
albums.description: The Velvet Underground's debut pairs Lou Reed's deadpan narration of drug deals and S&M with John Cale's droning electric viola and Sterling Morrison and Maureen Tucker's flat, tribal backing, while Andy Warhol-installed chanteuse Nico sings three tracks in her deep, accented monotone. Songs like 'Heroin' and 'Venus in Furs' turn taboo subject matter into hypnotic, minimally-chorded rock, and the extended noise breakdowns anticipate both punk and drone music decades early. Commercially ignored on release, it became the founding document for art-damaged, unglamorous rock songwriting.
albums.lineage: Grew out of Lou Reed's pop-song craft and John Cale's minimalist drone background, packaged by Andy Warhol; it is the direct root of glam, punk, No Wave, and the deadpan indie songwriting later carried by Jonathan Richman, Pavement, and Yo La Tengo.

albums.label: Elektra Records
albums.description: Arranged by John Cale, The Marble Index abandons Chelsea Girl's folk-pop entirely for Nico's own droning harmonium and Cale's stark, dissonant instrumental settings built around her voice and keyboard. Her voice is a flat, doom-laden drone across songs like 'Frozen Warnings', the tempos glacial and the mood bleak throughout. Commercially ignored at the time, it now sounds like a precursor of goth and dark-ambient songwriting, arriving years before those genres had names.
albums.lineage: John Cale's arrangements carry the Velvet Underground's drone directly into stark solo songwriting; the record sounds like a root of gothic rock and of the slow, glacial end of slowcore.

albums.label: Verve
albums.description: Recorded live in the studio at brutal volume, the Velvet Underground's second album buries Lou Reed's vocals under distortion and lets the band's noisiest instincts take over, climaxing in the 17-minute feedback jam 'Sister Ray,' cut in a single take. 'The Gift' splits the stereo channels between a deadpan spoken story and an instrumental drone, while the title track pounds along on distorted, barrelhouse piano. It is the loudest and most abrasive record the band made, and its willful ugliness became a blueprint for noise rock.
albums.lineage: Pushed the drone experiments of the first album to their extreme, setting a template that Sonic Youth, Swans, and other noise-rock and No Wave bands later followed.

albums.label: Elektra Records
albums.description: Produced by John Cale, whose viola drones through the raga-like ten-minute 'We Will Fall', the Stooges' debut otherwise strips rock down to its most primitive elements: simple riffs, Iggy Pop's yowled vocals, and blunt, repetitive song structures built for maximum physical impact. 'I Wanna Be Your Dog' rides a single sleigh-bell-and-three-chord hook, an act of deliberate, defiant primitivism that punk bands would take up a decade later. Cale's involvement is the direct thread tying the album's droning noise back to the Velvet Underground he had just left.
albums.lineage: John Cale's production is a direct, documented line from the Velvet Underground's drone experiments to Detroit proto-punk, and the album's raw, three-chord amateurism became a foundational text for punk rock itself.

albums.label: MGM
albums.description: With John Cale gone and Doug Yule in his place, the band's third album drops the feedback almost entirely for hushed, close-mic'd ballads like 'Pale Blue Eyes' and 'Candy Says,' Lou Reed's voice barely above a whisper over clean, interlocking guitars. Maureen Tucker takes a rare lead vocal on 'After Hours,' and 'The Murder Mystery' experiments with overlapping spoken-word tracks panned hard left and right. It is the quietest and most intimate Velvets record, trading confrontation for a tender, wounded stillness.
albums.lineage: Reacted directly against the noise of White Light/White Heat; Jonathan Richman was an avowed Velvets devotee, and slowcore acts like Low and Galaxie 500 and deadpan songwriters like Bill Callahan sound indebted to its quiet, guitar-based intimacy.

albums.label: Columbia Records
albums.description: John Cale's solo debut sets the Velvet Underground's drone almost entirely aside for concise, melodic pop, closer to the Byrds or late-'60s Van Morrison than to anything on White Light/White Heat. Cale sings in a warm, unassuming voice over jangling guitars and tight, economical arrangements, songs like 'Big White Cloud' and 'Adelaide' showing off a songwriting craft his avant-garde reputation had obscured. It is the gentlest, most accessible door into his catalog.
albums.lineage: Shows the Velvet Underground's classically trained member turning immediately toward pop songcraft, a strand of his work that later jangle and chamber-pop indie bands, drawing equally on drone and melody, sound indebted to.

albums.label: Reprise Records
albums.description: Co-produced by John Cale, Desertshore keeps the harmonium drone of The Marble Index but frames it in slightly warmer, more folk-adjacent arrangements, with Cale supplying much of the surrounding instrumentation. 'Janitor of Lunacy' and 'My Only Child' are sung in Nico's flat, funereal alto with sparse, hushed support that barely rises above a whisper. It is for listeners drawn to bleak, hymn-like stillness rather than songs with hooks.
albums.lineage: Continues the Cale-Nico partnership that turned Velvet Underground drone into stark solo song-form; hushed, harmonium- or organ-based indie and slowcore artists sound indebted to that approach.

albums.label: Cotillion (Atlantic)
albums.description: Made after Cale's exit and with Maureen Tucker absent, Loaded is the Velvet Underground's most conventional and hook-driven record, opening with the surging riff of 'Sweet Jane' and the celebratory 'Rock & Roll,' both built as radio-length songs. Doug Yule sings several songs, Lou Reed quit the band before its release, and the production is comparatively polished and major-key. Its two best-known songs entered the classic-rock canon.
albums.lineage: Strips the band's earlier drone and noise down to concise, guitar-driven pop songs; Yo La Tengo and the Feelies, both open Velvets admirers, and power pop from Big Star onward sound indebted to it.

albums.label: RCA Records
albums.description: Reed's solo debut re-records eight unreleased Velvet Underground-era songs with a crew of British session players, including members of Yes, smoothing the material's rough edges into a slicker, more conventional art-rock sound. 'Lisa Says' and 'Ocean' show off Reed's storytelling voice without the band's noise, but the polished arrangements mute some of the original tension, and the record was largely overshadowed by Transformer months later. It functions mostly as a transitional document, interesting for its versions of songs the Velvets never officially released.
albums.lineage: Marks Reed's first attempt to carry Velvet Underground songwriting into a solo career, a template of plainspoken narrative over conventional rock backing he refined across the rest of the decade.

albums.label: RCA Records
albums.description: Produced by David Bowie and Mick Ronson at the height of glam, Transformer wraps Lou Reed's deadpan tales of Warhol Factory hangers-on in string arrangements, saxophone, and hooky, almost cabaret-pop melodies. 'Walk on the Wild Side' turns a list of drag queens and hustlers into a loping, bass-led single, while 'Perfect Day' and 'Satellite of Love' soften Reed's sneer into genuine tenderness. It is the most approachable door into his solo catalog, for listeners who like their outsider New York portraits dressed in glam-pop gloss.
albums.lineage: Takes the Velvet Underground's deadpan character sketches and dresses them in glam-pop production by Bowie and Ronson; later art-pop and indie songwriters who mine outsider characters for empathy sound indebted to it.

albums.label: Cotillion
albums.description: Taped on a cassette recorder by Andy Warhol associate Brigid Polk during the band's 1970 residency at the New York club Max's Kansas City, this is a hissy, mono, deliberately unglamorous document of Lou Reed's final shows with the Velvet Underground. The band runs through 'Sweet Jane,' 'Pale Blue Eyes' and 'I'm Waiting for the Man' with a conversational looseness far removed from studio polish, audience chatter audible throughout. It is for listeners who want the Velvets as a small-room bar band.
albums.lineage: A bootleg-quality document of live-in-the-room recording; later cassette-culture and lo-fi indie acts like Guided by Voices and Daniel Johnston sound indebted to its unpolished aesthetic.

albums.label: Reprise Records
albums.description: Paris 1919 sets John Cale's warm baritone against lush orchestral pop arrangements, filled with references to Dylan Thomas and postwar European history but sung with a deceptively breezy, melodic ease. 'Child's Christmas in Wales' and the title track glide over strings and piano with an almost easy-listening surface that hides genuinely strange, literate lyrics underneath. It is Cale at his most purely melodic, a world away from his viola-drone work in the Velvet Underground but no less carefully constructed.
albums.lineage: Applies a Velvet Underground alumnus's classically trained arrangement skill to accessible pop songwriting, a combination that later chamber-pop and orchestral indie acts sound indebted to.

albums.label: RCA Records
albums.description: A bleak concept album about a doomed, drug-addicted couple, Berlin is scored with Bob Ezrin's orchestral rock-opera production, with weeping strings, horns and the sound of children crying on 'The Kids', Reed's voice sunk low and world-weary throughout. Songs like 'Caroline Says I' and 'The Bed' detail domestic abuse and suicide with a novelist's specificity, a tone critics dismissed in 1973 but reassessed decades later. Its slow tempos and unrelenting sadness make it an ancestor of the slowcore records that followed.
albums.lineage: Extends the Velvet Underground's interest in unglamorous, novelistic character studies into full-album form, a model later followed by concept-minded songwriters from the Mountain Goats to Sun Kil Moon.

albums.label: Island Records
albums.description: Nico's fourth album keeps her harmonium-and-drone sound but folds in synthesizers and electronic textures from Brian Eno, with John Cale producing and Roxy Music's Phil Manzanera adding guitar. The title track is a slow, mournful cover of the Doors' 'The End', sung in Nico's flattened deadpan over a queasy, echoing arrangement. It is the bleakest and most electronically textured of her Cale-era run, for listeners who want drone songwriting at its most desolate.
albums.lineage: Extends the Cale/Nico drone sound into early electronic textures, a mix of synth and harmonium drone that later post-punk and dream-pop acts sound indebted to.

albums.label: Mercury
albums.description: Compiled from 1969 club shows in Dallas and San Francisco, this double album catches the post-Cale lineup stretching songs well past their studio lengths, with long, patient versions of 'Heroin' and 'Ocean'. The performances are looser and warmer than the studio takes, Lou Reed's conversational vocals riding a band clearly comfortable playing for a small room. It is for listeners who want the Velvets as a working club band rather than an art project.
albums.lineage: Its long, exploratory live arrangements sound like a forerunner of the extended guitar jamming that Yo La Tengo and Sonic Youth would later build whole albums around.

albums.label: RCA Records
albums.description: After the confrontational Metal Machine Music, Coney Island Baby finds Reed unexpectedly tender, singing plainly over warm, unhurried electric and acoustic guitar interplay on songs like 'She's My Best Friend'. The long title track closes the record with a rambling, half-spoken monologue about wanting to play football for the coach, one of Reed's most disarmingly sincere vocal performances. It trades provocation for a hushed, late-night warmth, for listeners who prefer Reed romantic rather than confrontational.
albums.lineage: Shows the deadpan Velvet Underground storyteller turning inward toward quiet sincerity, a mode that hushed, plainspoken songwriters like Smog and Bill Callahan sound indebted to.

albums.label: RCA Records
albums.description: An hour of layered guitar feedback with no beat, melody, or vocal, Metal Machine Music was built by Lou Reed from amplifiers and effects set against each other and left to howl. RCA released it as though it were a rock record and it baffled most listeners, but its shifting overtones sit closer to minimalist drone composition than to anything on the pop charts. It is the most extreme extrapolation of the feedback experiments the Velvet Underground began on White Light/White Heat, for noise and drone listeners only.
albums.lineage: Carries the Velvet Underground's feedback drone to its logical, songless extreme, and noise and drone musicians have long claimed it as an early precedent for pure guitar noise as music.

albums.artist: Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers
albums.album: Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers
albums.label: Beserkley Records
albums.description: Released the same year the shelved 1972 tapes finally surfaced as The Modern Lovers, this second self-titled album is a different, gentler band entirely: Richman had by now turned away from electric drone-rock toward simpler, almost childlike songs, backed by a new lineup on light, unhurried rock and roll. Covers of older pop songs sit next to originals about ice cream trucks and the abominable snowman, Richman's deadpan sincerity turning material that could read as novelty into genuinely warm songwriting. It marks the start of his long turn away from Velvets-style drone toward the deliberately simple, lo-fi style he kept for the rest of his career.
albums.lineage: Shows Richman consciously stripping the Velvet Underground's noise out of his own sound, a move toward radical simplicity and lo-fi songwriting later mirrored by acts like Daniel Johnston and the Moldy Peaches.

albums.label: Beserkley Records
albums.description: Recorded in the early 1970s partly with John Cale producing but not released until 1976, The Modern Lovers channels Velvet Underground drone, a simple organ-and-bass pulse in the spirit of 'Sister Ray', into deadpan, wide-eyed songs about driving Massachusetts highways at night. Jonathan Richman sings in a flat, enthusiastic near-monotone over Jerry Harrison's droning organ and David Robinson's simple, propulsive drums, raw and all the more direct for it. 'Roadrunner' and 'Pablo Picasso' are the entry points for anyone tracing how punk and indie learned that you didn't need virtuosity.
albums.lineage: Richman was an avowed Velvet Underground devotee and John Cale produced some of these sessions; the Sex Pistols later played 'Roadrunner', making the record a documented bridge from the Velvets to punk.

albums.artist: Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers
albums.album: Rock 'n' Roll with the Modern Lovers
albums.label: Beserkley Records
albums.description: Richman pares the band down further here to acoustic guitar, upright bass and drums, treating traditional folk tunes and children's songs with the same flat, sincere delivery he gives his own compositions. The instrumental 'Egyptian Reggae' became an unlikely European hit single, its simple, sunny vamp a world away from the Velvet Underground's drone even as it keeps the same commitment to minimalism.
albums.lineage: Continues Richman's post-Velvets turn toward radical simplicity, an approach that fed directly into the amateurish, unpolished aesthetic later prized by lo-fi and slacker indie bands.

albums.label: Elektra Records
albums.description: Television's debut trades punk's power chords for long, interlocking lead lines between Tom Verlaine and Richard Lloyd, clean, chiming guitar tones with little of the distortion associated with the CBGB scene around them. The title track stretches past ten minutes, the guitars trading solos in a way closer to the Velvet Underground's extended workouts than to the Ramones' three-chord blasts. It is essential for anyone who loves guitar interplay more than guitar volume.
albums.lineage: Grew out of the same downtown New York scene the Velvet Underground had helped seed, and its interlocking guitar lines sound like a template for R.E.M., Sonic Youth, and the broader American college-rock guitar vocabulary.

albums.label: Arista Records
albums.description: Street Hassle mixes studio takes with live band recordings made using an early binaural technique, giving the record an unusually spatial, in-the-room feel. The eleven-minute title suite splices three linked stories over a looping cello figure, taking in a grim overdose tale and a brief spoken cameo from Bruce Springsteen. It is one of Reed's most structurally ambitious solo pieces, matching punk's rawness to novelistic, multi-part songwriting.
albums.lineage: Reed's most punk-adjacent solo record, made as the CBGB scene the Velvets had helped inspire was breaking; its blunt, live-sounding production and long-form storytelling sound like a forerunner of art-punk and slowcore alike.

albums.artist: Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers
albums.label: Beserkley Records
albums.description: Back in Your Life leans further into the doo-wop and children's-song influences Jonathan Richman had been exploring since leaving loud electric rock behind, with light, spare backing and plenty of room for his voice. Songs like 'Abdul and Cleopatra' and 'Party in the Woods Tonight' are delivered with the same wide-eyed, unguarded sincerity as his earlier work. It is for listeners who find his innocence charming rather than slight.
albums.lineage: Pushes Richman's post-Velvets embrace of simplicity and amateurism to its furthest point, prefiguring the deliberately childlike, lo-fi sensibility of artists like Daniel Johnston.

albums.label: RCA Records
albums.description: Reed's sharpest solo album in years pairs him with guitarist Robert Quine, whose jagged, wiry lead lines spar with Reed's own rhythm guitar on sparse, live-sounding arrangements. Songs like 'The Blue Mask' and 'Waves of Fear' turn confessional, sometimes violent imagery into tense rock, while 'Heavenly Arms' is a plain, unguarded love song. The interplay between the two guitarists gives the record a raw, conversational energy closer to CBGB than to Reed's glossier late-'70s work.
albums.lineage: Robert Quine, formerly of Richard Hell and the Voidoids, brought the downtown New York punk guitar vocabulary the Velvet Underground had helped seed back into Reed's solo sound.

albums.label: Verve
albums.description: Assembled from tracks the band recorded in 1968-69 for a shelved fourth MGM album, VU surfaced from the Polygram vaults over a decade after the band split and reveals a more accessible, straightforwardly melodic Velvet Underground than the finished albums suggested. Songs like 'Stephanie Says' and 'Ocean' are sung by Lou Reed in a warm, conversational register over clean, lightly strummed guitars. Several tracks here were later reworked by Reed on his solo albums, making this a good place to hear them in their leaner original form.
albums.lineage: A vault release that filled in the melodic, song-oriented side of the Velvets' catalog; several of its songs were later reworked on Lou Reed's solo records.

albums.label: Verve
albums.description: The leftover half of the same 1968-69 vault material that produced VU the year before, Another View is rawer and more scattered, pairing two versions of the drifting 'Hey Mr. Rain' with rough outtakes closer in spirit to White Light/White Heat. 'Ride Into the Sun' would later resurface, reworked, on Lou Reed's solo debut, and an early 'Rock and Roll' shows the band sketching a song they finished on Loaded. It is a scrappier listen than its companion volume, mainly for listeners who have exhausted the main albums.
albums.lineage: Documents the noisier, unfinished corners of the Velvets' late catalog and shows how directly Lou Reed mined the band's shelved material for his own solo records.
key_tracks: We're Gonna Have a Real Good Time Together

albums.label: Sire Records
albums.description: A deliberately stripped-down, two-guitars-bass-drums record, New York is Reed's state-of-the-city address, fourteen songs of blunt social commentary about AIDS, racism, and political corruption meant to be heard start to finish. 'Dirty Blvd.' and 'Romeo Had Juliette' pair plainspoken, almost journalistic lyrics with unfussy, live-sounding guitar rock, a return to directness after a decade of more polished records. It is the latter-day Reed album for listeners who want the unglamorous street detail of the first Velvet Underground record.
albums.lineage: Returns to the plain-spoken, street-level songwriting of the first Velvet Underground album, and its bare productions sound like a template for later songwriters who let lyrics, not arrangement, carry a record.

albums.label: Rounder Records
albums.description: I, Jonathan finds Jonathan Richman looking back at his own history, paying tribute to the band he idolized on 'Velvet Underground' and revisiting his most famous song on 'Roadrunner (Twice)'. The arrangements are sparse and unhurried, mostly acoustic guitar and light drums, his voice delivering plain, present-tense observations about parties, summer nights, and dancing on songs like 'That Summer Feeling'. It is a warm, funny entry point to his later catalog for anyone who loves the Modern Lovers.
albums.lineage: The song 'Velvet Underground' is an explicit tribute to the band Richman idolized, and the record's loose, unpretentious sound sits close to the 1990s lo-fi and slacker acts that treated him as a touchstone.
